data.name: Stage_Planning_Overline
data.value: Testing journey · 1

data.name: Stage_Planning_Title
data.value: Test planning

data.name: Stage_Planning_Lead
data.value: Decide what will be tested, how thoroughly, and what has to be true before anybody calls it done.

data.name: Stage_Planning_Why
data.value: Most teams do plan, in a document nobody opens again. The plan matters because it is the only place the words “enough testing” are ever given a meaning — and if that meaning is not written down before the work starts, it gets decided at the end, under pressure, by whoever is most tired.

data.name: Stage_Planning_Points
data.value: What test planning covers

data.name: Stage_Planning_Point1_Title
data.value: Scope and approach

data.name: Stage_Planning_Point1_Text
data.value: What is in, what is deliberately out, and how each part will be tested. The “deliberately out” half is the one that saves an argument later.

data.name: Stage_Planning_Point2_Title
data.value: Risks, rated

data.name: Stage_Planning_Point2_Text
data.value: What could go wrong, how likely it is and what it would cost. Testing effort follows that rating rather than following habit.

data.name: Stage_Planning_Point3_Title
data.value: Entry and exit criteria

data.name: Stage_Planning_Point3_Text
data.value: The conditions for starting and for stopping, agreed in advance and checked against reality at the end.

data.name: Stage_Planning_Today
data.value: Not built. Planning lives in the roadmap, not in the product: there is no plan editor, no risk register and no criteria to check against. The pages above describe what is intended, not what you can use.

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Overline
data.value: Testing journey · 2

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Title
data.value: Test analysis and traceability

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Lead
data.value: Turn requirements into things that can actually be checked, and keep the thread from each requirement to the tests that cover it.

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Why
data.value: A requirement that cannot be checked is not a requirement, it is a hope. Reading requirements for testability is the cheapest defect-finding there is: it costs an afternoon and it finds the contradictions before anybody has written code against them.

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Points
data.value: What analysis covers

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Point1_Title
data.value: Testability review

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Point1_Text
data.value: Each requirement read for the things that make it untestable: a missing number, an undefined “fast”, two sentences that cannot both be true.

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Point2_Title
data.value: Test conditions

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Point2_Text
data.value: The distinct things worth checking about a requirement, named before anybody writes a step. This is where coverage is decided.

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Point3_Title
data.value: A traceability matrix that is not a spreadsheet

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Point3_Text
data.value: Requirements against tests, with the gaps visible, kept current because it is derived rather than maintained by hand.

data.name: Stage_Analysis_Today
data.value: Not built. There is no requirement, no test condition and no matrix in the product yet. The data model for them is designed and written down; none of it is running.

data.name: Stage_Design_Overline
data.value: Testing journey · 3

data.name: Stage_Design_Title
data.value: Test design

data.name: Stage_Design_Lead
data.value: Work out the actual cases: which inputs, which boundaries, which combinations, and what data they need.

data.name: Stage_Design_Why
data.value: Test design is where testing stops being a feeling and becomes a technique. Boundary values, equivalence classes, decision tables and state transitions are not academic: they are the difference between forty tests that all check the same thing and twelve that check twelve different things.

data.name: Stage_Design_Points
data.value: What design covers

data.name: Stage_Design_Point1_Title
data.value: Techniques, applied deliberately

data.name: Stage_Design_Point1_Text
data.value: Boundaries, equivalence classes, decision tables, state transitions — chosen for the problem rather than used out of habit.

data.name: Stage_Design_Point2_Title
data.value: Cases a person can read

data.name: Stage_Design_Point2_Text
data.value: Steps, expected results and the reason the case exists, versioned, so a change to a test is as reviewable as a change to code.

data.name: Stage_Design_Point3_Title
data.value: Test data

data.name: Stage_Design_Point3_Text
data.value: What each case needs to exist before it runs, described with the case instead of being improvised on the day.

data.name: Stage_Design_Today
data.value: Not built. No test case library and no AI-assisted design exist in the product. A planner that turns a scenario in plain words into executable steps does exist and is measured — see the capability page — but it is not case design.

data.name: Stage_Execution_Overline
data.value: Testing journey · 4

data.name: Stage_Execution_Title
data.value: Test execution

data.name: Stage_Execution_Lead
data.value: Run the tests against a real application in a real browser, and keep enough evidence that a failure can be acted on without being reproduced first.

data.name: Stage_Execution_Why
data.value: A run that says “failed” and nothing else sends a person back to reproduce it, which is where most of the cost of a defect is. A run worth having names the step, keeps the screenshot of the moment it went wrong, and distinguishes the application being broken from the test infrastructure being broken.

data.name: Stage_Execution_Points
data.value: What execution covers

data.name: Stage_Execution_Point1_Title
data.value: Every ending has its own name

data.name: Stage_Execution_Point1_Text
data.value: Passed, failed, stopped, out of time, over budget, could not run. A run that hit its budget is not a failing application, and calling it one would make the failure rate a lie.

data.name: Stage_Execution_Point2_Title
data.value: Evidence, kept per step

data.name: Stage_Execution_Point2_Text
data.value: A screenshot and a timestamp for each step, so the failure arrives with the picture of what the application actually showed.

data.name: Stage_Execution_Point3_Title
data.value: The browser runs where it cannot reach anything

data.name: Stage_Execution_Point3_Text
data.value: Out of process, behind a proxy that refuses every address but the one being tested, judging where a connection actually goes rather than what it is called.

data.name: Stage_Execution_Today
data.value: Built, and the only stage that is. A browser is driven against a real application out of process, runs are stored with their steps and screenshots, and one organization cannot see another’s. What is not built: a container for each run, and any target other than our own demo application.

data.name: Stage_Defects_Overline
data.value: Testing journey · 5

data.name: Stage_Defects_Title
data.value: Defect management

data.name: Stage_Defects_Lead
data.value: Report what went wrong so that somebody can fix it, and keep the link back to the test and the requirement it came from.

data.name: Stage_Defects_Why
data.value: Most of the time lost to a defect is spent on the round trip: a report too thin to act on, a developer who cannot reproduce it, a tester who has moved on. A defect raised out of a run already carries the steps, the evidence and the environment, which removes the round trip rather than speeding it up.

data.name: Stage_Defects_Points
data.value: What defect management covers

data.name: Stage_Defects_Point1_Title
data.value: Raised from the run

data.name: Stage_Defects_Point1_Text
data.value: The failing step, its screenshot and its timings become the report, so nothing has to be described twice or from memory.

data.name: Stage_Defects_Point2_Title
data.value: A lifecycle somebody agreed to

data.name: Stage_Defects_Point2_Text
data.value: Triage, severity and status that mean the same thing to everyone, with the history of who changed what kept.

data.name: Stage_Defects_Point3_Title
data.value: Links in both directions

data.name: Stage_Defects_Point3_Text
data.value: From the defect to the test, the requirement and the run; and from a requirement to every defect found against it.

data.name: Stage_Defects_Today
data.value: Not built. A failed run keeps its step, message and screenshot, which is the raw material; there is no defect record, no triage and no synchronisation with an issue tracker.

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Overline
data.value: Testing journey · 6

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Title
data.value: Reporting and release readiness

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Lead
data.value: Say what the testing found, what it did not cover, and whether the exit criteria agreed at the start have actually been met.

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Why
data.value: The question at the end is always the same: do we ship? A report answers it badly by counting tests, and well by comparing what was found against what was agreed — including the parts nobody tested, which is the number most reports quietly leave out.

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Points
data.value: What reporting covers

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Point1_Title
data.value: Coverage, including its gaps

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Point1_Text
data.value: What was tested against what was planned, with the untested parts named rather than omitted.

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Point2_Title
data.value: Trends, not snapshots

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Point2_Text
data.value: How results, flake and defect ages move over releases, because one run tells you almost nothing.

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Point3_Title
data.value: A readiness decision with its reasons attached

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Point3_Text
data.value: The exit criteria, which of them hold, and who signed it off — kept, so the decision can be reviewed afterwards.

data.name: Stage_Reporting_Today
data.value: Not built. Runs are stored, so the data a report would draw on is beginning to exist; there are no dashboards, no trends and no readiness report.

data.name: Product_Principles_Title
data.value: Three things we will not trade away

data.name: Product_Principles_Intro
data.value: Every product makes trade-offs. These are the ones we have decided in advance, written down, and held ourselves to with tests.

data.name: Product_Principle_Traceability_Title
data.value: A result you can trace back

data.name: Product_Principle_Traceability_Text
data.value: A verdict is only worth something if you can see what it was based on: which steps ran, against what, and what the application actually showed.

data.name: Product_Principle_Bounded_Title
data.value: A model that plans, never one that acts freely

data.name: Product_Principle_Bounded_Text
data.value: Where AI is used, it chooses from a fixed set of browser actions and its output is checked before anything runs. No model output is ever executed as code.

data.name: Product_Principle_Evidence_Title
data.value: Numbers before claims

data.name: Product_Principle_Evidence_Text
data.value: We publish what we measured, including what we have not measured yet. A capability without numbers is described as a plan.

data.name: Product_State_Title
data.value: What you can use today

data.name: Product_State_Lead
data.value: One of the six stages is built: test execution.

data.name: Product_State_Text
data.value: Accounts, organisations, roles and the audit trail are real. Execution drives a browser against an application and keeps the evidence. The other five stages are designed and written down, and none of them is running. We would rather tell you that here than in a demonstration.

data.name: Product_State_Link
data.value: See what execution does, in detail

data.name: Capabilities_MetaDescription
data.value: What the platform can test, and how a new kind of testing is added to it.

data.name: Capabilities_Title
data.value: Capabilities: what kind of testing a run actually does

data.name: Capabilities_Lead
data.value: The journey is the same whatever you are testing. What changes is the kind of test, and each kind is a plug-in.

data.name: Capabilities_What_Text
data.value: A capability is one kind of testing: it knows how to start a run, what to show while the run happens, and how to present the result. Everything around it — plans, requirements, cases, defects, reports — is shared.

data.name: Capabilities_Why_Text
data.value: The reason to build it this way is that the hard parts are not specific to web testing: traceability, evidence, tenancy and honest reporting are the same problems for an API test or a performance test. Getting them right once is the point of the structure.

data.name: Capabilities_List_Title
data.value: What exists, and what does not

data.name: Capabilities_Web_Title
data.value: Web end-to-end testing

data.name: Capabilities_Web_Text
data.value: A real browser driven against a web application, out of process, behind a proxy that refuses every address but the one being tested. Built, with its own page of detail.

data.name: Capabilities_Web_Action
data.value: How it works

data.name: Capabilities_Api_Title
data.value: API testing

data.name: Capabilities_Api_Text
data.value: Requests, schemas and contracts. Designed as a capability; not written.

data.name: Capabilities_Performance_Title
data.value: Performance testing

data.name: Capabilities_Performance_Text
data.value: Load profiles and response budgets. Designed as a capability; not written.

data.name: Capabilities_Security_Title
data.value: Security testing

data.name: Capabilities_Security_Text
data.value: Known-vulnerability checks and misconfiguration scans. Designed as a capability; not written.

data.name: Capabilities_Accessibility_Title
data.value: Accessibility testing

data.name: Capabilities_Accessibility_Text
data.value: Automated WCAG checks inside a run. We do this to our own site on every change; it is not a capability you can use yet.

data.name: E2E_MetaDescription
data.value: A real browser driven against a web application, with a screenshot of every step and a failure you can act on.

data.name: E2E_Overline
data.value: Capability

data.name: E2E_Title
data.value: A browser, driven against your application, where it cannot reach anything else

data.name: E2E_Lead
data.value: This is the part of the product that is finished. It opens a real browser, carries out a sequence of steps against a web application, and keeps a screenshot and a timestamp for each one.

data.name: E2E_How_Title
data.value: What happens when a run starts

data.name: E2E_How_Intro
data.value: Four things, in this order, every time.

data.name: E2E_How_Step1_Title
data.value: The run is queued and claimed

data.name: E2E_How_Step1_Text
data.value: The run is a row in the database before it is anything else, so it survives a restart and two machines cannot take the same one.

data.name: E2E_How_Step2_Title
data.value: A worker starts, knowing almost nothing

data.name: E2E_How_Step2_Text
data.value: It is given a run id, a target, a budget and a directory. It is never told which organisation the run belongs to, so a worker a hostile page has taken over learns one run and nothing about any other customer.

data.name: E2E_How_Step3_Title
data.value: Each step runs, and leaves its evidence

data.name: E2E_How_Step3_Text
data.value: A screenshot at the end of every step, with the times it started and finished. Password fields are painted over before the picture is taken.

data.name: E2E_How_Step4_Title
data.value: The result is written back under the right tenant

data.name: E2E_How_Step4_Text
data.value: The worker returns a result naming its run; the application looks that run up, takes the organisation from the stored row, and writes under it. A result that names a different run is recorded as an infrastructure error rather than believed.

data.name: E2E_Boundary_Title
data.value: Where the browser is allowed to go

data.name: E2E_Boundary_Intro
data.value: A browser runs content written by somebody else. That is what browsers are for, and it is why this part was designed before any of it was built.

data.name: E2E_Boundary_Process_Title
data.value: Out of the application

data.name: E2E_Boundary_Process_Text
data.value: The browser runs in a separate process with no database connection and no credentials beyond the one run it is doing.

data.name: E2E_Boundary_Proxy_Title
data.value: One route out, which refuses by default

data.name: E2E_Boundary_Proxy_Text
data.value: Every connection goes through a proxy that judges the address it actually resolves to, on every hop of a redirect. That is what stops a name that points at an internal address.

data.name: E2E_Boundary_Tenant_Title
data.value: Evidence belongs to one organisation

data.name: E2E_Boundary_Tenant_Text
data.value: Screenshots are stored per organisation and reached only through a short-lived signed link issued after the ordinary permission check. Another organisation’s evidence is not refused — it does not exist.

data.name: E2E_Ai_Title
data.value: Where AI comes into it

data.name: E2E_Ai_Lead
data.value: A model can turn a scenario written in your words into the steps a run carries out. It plans once, before the browser opens, and is not involved while the run happens.

data.name: E2E_Ai_Text
data.value: Its output is a list of actions drawn from a fixed vocabulary — click, type, wait, check and a few more — and there is no field in which a script or a selector could be written. The plan is then checked: an action that does not exist, a path that could name another site, or a plan that checks nothing is refused before the browser starts.

data.name: E2E_Ai_Measured_Title
data.value: What we have measured, and what we have not

data.name: E2E_Ai_Measured_Text
data.value: The hand-written baseline is measured: twelve controlled scenarios, half of them against a deliberately broken application, 36 runs, every verdict correct and no run passing an application that was broken. The planner’s own numbers do not exist yet, so we make no claim about what a model finds. When they exist they will be published next to the baseline, including the number that matters most: how often it says "passed" about an application that is not working.

data.name: E2E_NotYet_Title
data.value: What is not built yet

data.name: E2E_NotYet_Container
data.value: A container for each run. The browser runs in its own process, which is the right shape but not an isolation boundary — a process is not a sandbox.

data.name: E2E_NotYet_Targets
data.value: Any target other than our own demo application. Before a run may point at your site, there has to be a way to prove the site is yours.

data.name: E2E_NotYet_Storage
data.value: Object storage, retention and redaction for evidence. Screenshots live in a directory today.

data.name: E2E_NotYet_Why
data.value: These are on the list in that order, and the first of them is the reason a customer-supplied target is not offered yet.

data.name: Integrations_MetaDescription
data.value: Planned connections to Git, issue trackers and CI systems. Nothing here is built yet.

data.name: Integrations_Placeholder
data.value: No integration is built. This page lists what is intended, so the shape of the product is clear; none of it works today.

data.name: Integrations_Title
data.value: Integrations

data.name: Integrations_Lead
data.value: Testing is not a separate activity, so the tool cannot be a separate island. These are the connections that matter and the order we expect to build them in.

data.name: Integrations_Planned_Title
data.value: What is planned

data.name: Integrations_Planned_Intro
data.value: Each of these is a plan with nothing behind it yet.

data.name: Security_MetaDescription
data.value: How one customer is kept apart from another, where the browser is allowed to go, and what is not in place yet.

data.name: Security_Title
data.value: Security and trust

data.name: Security_Lead
data.value: A testing platform holds screenshots of your application, credentials for it, and the right to open a browser against it. This page says what protects each of those, and what does not yet.

data.name: Security_Tenancy_Title
data.value: Keeping one customer apart from another

data.name: Security_Tenancy_Intro
data.value: Three independent layers, because one of them being wrong should not be enough.

data.name: Security_Tenancy_Filter_Title
data.value: Every read is filtered

data.name: Security_Tenancy_Filter_Text
data.value: Queries are scoped to the signed-in organisation by the data layer itself, not by each query remembering to. Another organisation’s record is not refused; it does not exist.

data.name: Security_Tenancy_Write_Title
data.value: Every write is checked

data.name: Security_Tenancy_Write_Text
data.value: A save that would write a row into another organisation is refused by an interceptor that does not depend on the code above it being correct.

data.name: Security_Tenancy_Keys_Title
data.value: The database refuses it too

data.name: Security_Tenancy_Keys_Text
data.value: Related rows carry the organisation in their foreign key, so a child record cannot point at a parent in another organisation even if everything above it is wrong.

data.name: Security_Browser_Title
data.value: The browser that runs your tests

data.name: Security_Browser_Intro
data.value: It executes content chosen by whoever wrote the application under test, which is the condition browser escapes are written for.

data.name: Security_Browser_Process_Title
data.value: No database, no cloud role

data.name: Security_Browser_Process_Text
data.value: The worker has no connection to our data and no ambient credentials. It receives one job and returns one result.

data.name: Security_Browser_Egress_Title
data.value: Addresses, not names

data.name: Security_Browser_Egress_Text
data.value: The proxy judges where a connection actually resolves to, every time, including after a redirect. A hostname allowlist cannot do that.

data.name: Security_Browser_Model_Title
data.value: The worker holds no model key

data.name: Security_Browser_Model_Text
data.value: Planning happens on our side, before the browser opens. An attacker who owned one run could not spend our model budget on every other one.

data.name: Security_Data_Title
data.value: What is held, and where

data.name: Security_Data_Where_Label
data.value: Your data

data.name: Security_Data_Where_Text
data.value: One PostgreSQL database with every organisation’s rows filtered apart. A buyer who requires physical separation should ask us: that is a trade-off we made deliberately and wrote down.

data.name: Security_Data_Evidence_Label
data.value: Screenshots

data.name: Security_Data_Evidence_Text
data.value: A screenshot of your application may contain real names and real orders, so it is treated as personal data: stored per organisation, never public, reached only through a short-lived signed link. Password fields are masked before the picture is taken.

data.name: Security_Data_Credentials_Label
data.value: Credentials for your application

data.name: Security_Data_Credentials_Text
data.value: A run that signs in has to type a password into your application, so it is exposed to that application by necessity. It is not exposed anywhere else: a plan refers to a credential by name and never contains one.

data.name: Security_Data_Model_Label
data.value: What a model sees

data.name: Security_Data_Model_Text
data.value: When planning is used, the model is given the scenario and a description of the pages a crawl found — roles, names and visible text. It is never given a credential, an organisation or a run.

data.name: Security_NotYet_Title
data.value: What is not in place yet

data.name: Security_NotYet_Intro
data.value: A security page that lists only strengths is a sales document. These are the gaps we know about and would raise ourselves in a questionnaire.

data.name: Security_NotYet_Container
data.value: A container per run. The browser is a separate process, which is not the same thing as a sandbox.

data.name: Security_NotYet_Hosting
data.value: A stated hosting region. We intend EU hosting; there is nothing to point at yet, so we are not claiming it.

data.name: Security_NotYet_Certification
data.value: Any certification. No ISO 27001, no SOC 2, no audit. We will say so when that changes.

data.name: Security_NotYet_Audit
data.value: An append-only guarantee for the audit trail that holds outside the application. It cannot be edited through the product; database access is another matter.

data.name: About_Why_Title
data.value: Why this exists

data.name: About_Why_Lead
data.value: Testing tools are good at counting tests and bad at saying whether the software works.

data.name: About_Why_Text1
data.value: The number most tools put on the front page is a pass rate, and a pass rate mostly measures how many tests exist. A suite of four hundred tests that all check the same happy path passes beautifully, and tells a release manager nothing. The questions that matter are harder to display: what was not tested, which failures are the application and which are the test environment, and whether anything that passed should not have.

data.name: About_Why_Text2
data.value: Adding a model to a tool like that makes the problem worse rather than better, because a model will cheerfully produce a test that passes. So this product is being built in the opposite order: the evidence and the boundaries first, the model afterwards, and no claim about what the model can do until the number for how often it wrongly says “passed” has been measured and published.

data.value: What we commit to, how it is tested on every change, what is still missing, and how to tell us we have failed.

data.name: Access_Title
data.value: Accessibility

data.name: Access_Lead
data.value: This is the one statement on this site that is not a placeholder, because it is the only one we can verify ourselves.

data.name: Access_Standard_Title
data.value: What we aim for

data.name: Access_Standard_Text
data.value: WCAG 2.2 at level AA, on the public website and in the product. We aim for it rather than claim it, because a conformance claim needs an audit by somebody other than the people who wrote the code, and there has not been one.

data.name: Access_How_Title
data.value: How it is checked

data.name: Access_How_Intro
data.value: Not by intention. These checks run on every change and fail the build:

data.name: Access_How_Automated
data.value: An automated accessibility scan of every page, in the light and the dark theme, with zero serious or critical findings allowed.

data.name: Access_How_Keyboard
data.value: Keyboard tests: every control reachable, a visible focus ring, and a skip link to the main content.

data.name: Access_How_Contrast
data.value: Contrast checked against the tokens rather than per page, so a new page cannot introduce an unreadable combination.

data.name: Access_How_Motion
data.value: Reduced motion respected: animation is removed, not merely shortened, when the system asks for it.

data.name: Access_How_Status
data.value: Status is never conveyed by colour alone — a failing test run says the word as well as showing the colour.

data.name: Access_How_Limit
data.value: An automated scan finds perhaps a third to a half of real accessibility problems. It cannot tell whether a heading structure makes sense or whether an error message is useful, which is why the limitations below matter.

data.name: Access_Known_Title
data.value: Known limitations

data.name: Access_Known_Intro
data.value: Stated rather than discovered by you:

data.name: Access_Known_Manual
data.value: No screen-reader testing by a person who relies on one, and no external audit. Both are needed before any conformance claim.

data.name: Access_Known_German
data.value: The German translation has not been reviewed by a native speaker. A clumsy sentence is an accessibility problem for somebody reading with assistive technology.

data.name: Access_Known_App
data.value: The product behind the sign-in is tested the same way, but it is early, and a part of it that does not exist cannot have been checked.

data.name: Access_Feedback_Title
data.value: If something here does not work for you

data.name: Access_Feedback_Text
data.value: Tell us what you were trying to do, on which page, and with what — browser, screen reader, keyboard only. A specific report is worth more than a general one and we will answer it.

data.name: Access_Feedback_Action
data.value: Report an accessibility problem

data.name: Access_Feedback_Legal
data.value: In Germany, the Barrierefreiheitsstärkungsgesetz will require this of a service like ours. We would rather be ready early than compliant late.
